title: Review: Chromatography; Electrode potentials and the SHE; Measuring rates; Concentration–time graphs, half-life and clock reactions
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: KN05#t4 term and clue written for the game; RX04#t4 term and clue written for the game; KN05#t3 term and clue written for the game; KN01#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AN05#N.12, KN01#N.8a, KN05#N.11, RX04#N.10a, AN05#N.4, KN01#N.3a, KN05#N.12a, RX04#N.13, AN05#N.13, RX04#N.4a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Second order
items.clue: Rate against concentration curves upward ever more steeply; each halving takes longer.

items.label: Potential difference
items.clue: What is measured between two half-cells; one half-cell alone can never give a reading.

items.label: First order
items.clue: Rate against concentration is a straight line through the origin; halving time is constant.

items.label: Tangent
items.clue: A straight line drawn at one time on the curve; its gradient gives the rate at that instant.

questions.stem: A gas chromatogram of a mixture of three esters, P, Q and R, gives peak areas P 2.4, Q 3.6 and R 6.0 (arbitrary units). Assume the detector responds equally to each ester. What is the percentage of Q in the mixture?
A student reacts 0.10 g of magnesium ribbon with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Which method is least suitable for measuring the rate of this reaction?

options.text: Collecting the hydrogen in a gas syringe and reading the volume every 10 s
Recording the loss in mass of the flask on a balance every 10 s
Taking samples at timed intervals, quenching them and titrating the acid left
Timing how long it takes to collect the first 20 cm³ of hydrogen in a gas syringe

questions.explanation: H₂ has a tiny molar mass: 0.10 g of Mg gives only about 0.008 g of H₂. A typical balance can barely detect the total loss, let alone the changes between readings.

questions.stem: In an iodine clock, the blue-black colour appears after 48 s. A second run uses double the concentration of I⁻, with everything else the same, and the colour appears after 24 s. What is the order with respect to I⁻?

options.text: Zero order, as the same amount of iodine forms in both runs.
Order −1, as the time halves when [I⁻] doubles.
Second order, as [I⁻] doubles and the time halves: a factor of 2 × 2.
First order, as 1/t doubles when [I⁻] doubles.

questions.explanation: Rate ∝ 1/t. Doubling [I⁻] doubles 1/t, so the rate is proportional to [I⁻]: first order.

questions.stem: Standard electrode potentials: Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Mg(s), E° = −2.37 V · Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s), E° = −0.76 V · Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), E° = +0.34 V · Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s), E° = +0.80 V. Which species is the strongest oxidising agent?

options.text: Mg²⁺(aq), as its E° value is the largest in size
Mg(s), as it is the species most readily oxidised
Ag⁺(aq), as its E° value is the most positive
Ag(s), as silver has the most positive E° value

questions.explanation: Ag⁺ (+0.80 V) accepts electrons most readily, so it is the strongest oxidising agent listed.

questions.stem: The dyes in a black ink are separated by paper chromatography. Which difference between the dyes is mainly responsible for the separation?

options.text: The molar mass of each dye, because lighter dye molecules are carried faster
The strength of the attractions among the molecules of each dye on its own
The relative strength of each dye's attractions to the paper and to the solvent
The size of each dye's particles, because the paper holds back the larger ones

questions.explanation: A dye moves only while dissolved in the solvent. A dye held more strongly by the paper spends more time stationary and travels a shorter distance.

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Which quantity is the rate of this reaction at a particular moment?

options.text: The total time taken for all of the H₂O₂ in the sample to decompose
The total volume of O₂ given off by the time the reaction has stopped
The decrease in the concentration of H₂O₂ per unit time at that moment
The concentration of H₂O₂ at that moment divided by the time elapsed so far

questions.explanation: Rate is the change in concentration per unit time, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. At a moment, it is the gradient of the tangent, quoted as positive.

questions.stem: A hypothetical compound X decomposes at constant temperature. Results: t = 0, 200, 400, 600 s; [X] = 0.640, 0.320, 0.160, 0.080 mol dm⁻³. A new run at the same temperature starts at [X] = 0.320 mol dm⁻³. How long does [X] take to fall to 0.080 mol dm⁻³?
questions.explanation: [X] halves every 200 s, whatever the start: first order. 0.320 → 0.160 → 0.080 is two halvings: 400 s.

questions.stem: A standard Pb²⁺/Pb half-cell is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode. The voltmeter reads 0.13 V. The lead electrode is the negative electrode. Which statement is correct?

options.text: E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = +0.13 V, because the voltmeter reading gives the lead electrode's potential directly, sign included.
E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = −0.13 V, which is the absolute potential of the lead electrode on its own.
E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = −0.13 V; the reading is the difference from the hydrogen electrode, which is 0 V by convention.
No reaction happens at the hydrogen electrode, because its E° is 0 V.

questions.explanation: A single half-cell cannot be measured alone. The SHE is defined as 0 V, so the whole 0.13 V is assigned to lead; lead is oxidised (it supplies the electrons), so its E° is negative.

questions.stem: A student runs TLC of a mixture of two polar compounds on a silica plate, using hexane as the solvent. Both spots barely leave the origin. Which change is most likely to make the spots move further up the plate and separate?

options.text: Use a longer plate and let the hexane run twice as far.
Use a solvent that is even less polar than hexane.
Spot a more concentrated sample of the mixture.
Mix some ethyl ethanoate into the hexane.

questions.explanation: Ethyl ethanoate makes the mobile phase more polar. It attracts the polar compounds more strongly, so they spend more time dissolved and less time held by the silica. They move further.

questions.stem: Why is the standard electrode potential of the hydrogen half-cell, 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g), given as 0 V?

options.text: No oxidation or reduction occurs at the hydrogen electrode.
Its absolute potential has been measured directly and found to be zero.
It is assigned by convention as the reference for other half-cells.
The platinum electrode is inert, so no potential develops.

questions.explanation: Only potential differences can be measured, so one half-cell must be chosen as the reference and given a value. By convention it is the SHE, at 0 V.
